newsitem.title: USA: NYS Gov. blasts Assembly for risking prison funds.
newsitem.headline: NYS Gov. blasts Assembly for risking prison funds.

text.p: New York State Governor George Pataki on Tuesday blasted the Democrat-led Assembly, saying its failure to support ending parole for violent criminals was putting $100 million of federal aid at risk.

The Republican governor said the Department of Justice had advised his Administration that the state's failure to enact his "Truth in Sentencing" proposal by a July 1 deadline would cost the state $100 million of matching aid from Washington over four years.

Noting that state Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, had failed to deliver on a promise to approve stiffer sentences for juenvile criminals, Pataki said: "The Assembly Democrats have also indicated that they oppose eliminating parole for first-time murderers, rapists, and other violent criminals, even though millions of dollars of Federal funding hangs in the balance."
"That is unacceptable both on fiscal and public safety grounds," Pataki said.

Pataki's plan to sell $650 million of revenue bonds to pay for new prisons has been attacked as too costly and as unconstitutional by state Assemblyman Daniel Feldman, D-Brooklyn, and by the League of Women Voters for New York State.
A spokesman for Pataki has disputed these arguments.

The issue is an important one politically for Pataki, as Upstate communities, which tend to be Republican strongholds, are expected to request that the new prisons be built in their areas, in order to get new jobs.
Speaker Silver fired back at an Albany news conference held shortly after Pataki's.

Saying that at present more than 60 percent of the people in the state's jails were non-violent felons, Silver noted the federal funds were designated strictly for building prisons, a policy the Assembly did not support.

"It can't be used for maintenance," he said, referring to Washington's restriction on how its dollars would be spent. "The first point is that the Assembly budget does not contemplate prison construction, and therefore we would not be eligible for the $25 million (a year) if we don't construct."
Silver said that the Assembly had approved laws raising the sentences for sex offenders, assailants and the most violent offenders.

"We believe that parole is appropriate for people to end their prison sentences and go back to communities," he said, adding the Assembly wanted to use its existing jails for the most violent offenders.
